cards.title: Namaste opens every door
cards.body: नमस्ते (namaste) is hello, goodbye, and good morning rolled into one. It comes from Sanskrit: 'I bow to the divine in you.' Use it with anyone, anywhere, and doors open.

cards.title: Devanagari reads left to right
cards.body: Hindi is written in Devanagari, which reads left to right like English. The big difference: every consonant carries a built-in 'a' sound. क is not 'k' — it's 'ka'. A small slash called a halant (्) kills the 'a' when you don't want it.

Meet the vowels: अ (a) आ (aa) इ (i) ई (ee) उ (u) ऊ (oo) ए (e) ऐ (ai) ओ (o) औ (au). These ten vowels combine with every consonant. क + ी becomes की (kee). Once you know ten vowels and the consonants, you can sound out almost any word.
Don't memorize the whole script chart at once. Learn five letters a day and write real words with them — your hand remembers what your eyes forget.

cards.explain: Namaste works as hello, goodbye, and good morning — the all-purpose greeting. Good night is शुभ रात्रि (shubh raatri), thank you is धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad).

flashcards.back: Hello / goodbye — the universal Hindi greeting.
The consonant क carries a built-in 'a' sound — it's 'ka', not 'k'.

questions.explain: Devanagari reads left to right, same direction as English. (Arabic and Urdu read right to left — a common mix-up.)

questions.q: What sound does the consonant क make on its own?
questions.explain: Every Devanagari consonant carries an inherent 'a'. क is 'ka' until a halant or vowel mark changes it.

questions.q: Someone says नमस्ते to you. You reply…
questions.explain: Namaste answers namaste. अलविदा (alvida) is a farewell, धन्यवाद is thank you — both fine words, wrong moment.

questions.q: What does the halant mark (्) do?
choices: Marks the end of a sentence
questions.explain: The halant silences the inherent 'a'. That's how क (ka) becomes क् (k) when you need a pure consonant.
धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad) is thank you. नमस्ते is hello, हाँ (haan) is yes.

cards.title: Verbs end in -ना
cards.body: Almost every Hindi infinitive ends in ना (naa): करना (karnaa, to do), जाना (jaanaa, to go), खाना (khaanaa, to eat), पीना (peenaa, to drink). Spot the ना ending and you've found the verb.

cards.title: Present tense is beautifully regular
cards.body: Drop the ना, add ता/ती/ते. मैं खाता हूँ (main khaataa hoon) = I eat (male speaker). मैं खाती हूँ (main khaatee hoon) = I eat (female speaker). The verb ending changes with the speaker's gender — the first real twist of Hindi.

वह जाता है (vah jaataa hai) — He goes.
वह जाती है (vah jaatee hai) — She goes.
हम खाते हैं (ham khaate hain) — We eat.

Swap the ending, keep the root. जा (jaa) is the root of जाना; खा (khaa) is the root of खाना.
Learn verbs in pairs with their opposites: आना (to come) / जाना (to go), खाना (to eat) / पीना (to drink). Opposites stick together in memory.

cards.q: मैं पीता हूँ (main peetaa hoon) means…
cards.explain: पीता (peetaa) is the masculine present form of पीना, and हूँ marks 'I'. So: I drink, said by a man.

flashcards.back: The frame for 'I ___' in the present tense — drop the verb root in the middle.

questions.q: How do you spot a Hindi infinitive?
questions.explain: The ना ending is the infinitive marker: करना, जाना, खाना. It's the dictionary form of the verb.

questions.q: वह खाती है (vah khaatee hai) — who is eating?
questions.explain: The ती (tee) ending marks feminine. खाती = she eats. Masculine would be खाता (khaataa).

questions.q: What is the root of जाना (to go)?
questions.explain: Drop the ना infinitive ending and जा remains. The root is what you build tenses on.
Both are opposites — come/go and eat/drink. Learning verbs in opposite pairs is the fastest way to double your vocabulary.

questions.q: मैं जाता हूँ uses हूँ because…
questions.explain: हूँ (hoon) is the 'I' form of होना (to be). मैं (main) = I, so the sentence needs हूँ to agree.

cards.title: Introduce yourself in one line
cards.body: मेरा नाम ___ है (meraa naam ___ hai) — My name is ___. और आप? (aur aap?) — And you? That's a whole introduction. आप (aap) is the respectful 'you'; तुम (tum) is for friends and kids.

cards.title: Ask like a local
cards.body: कितने का है? (kitne kaa hai?) — How much is it? कहाँ है…? (kahaan hai…?) — Where is…? Two questions that survive any market, station, or street in India.

A: आप कैसे हैं? (aap kaise hain?) — How are you?
B: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। (main theek hoon, dhanyavaad.) — I'm fine, thank you.
और आप? (aur aap?) — And you?

Memorize this exchange whole. It's the most common conversation in Hindi.
Hindi speakers love it when learners try. Even broken Hindi with a smile gets warmer responses than perfect English — effort is the whole game.

cards.q: You're shopping. The price matters. You ask…
cards.explain: कितने का है means 'how much is it' — the market question. The others ask your name and where the market is.

questions.q: Why use आप (aap) instead of तुम (tum) with strangers?
choices: आप is respectful; तुम is familiar
questions.explain: आप is the respectful 'you' for strangers and elders. तुम is for friends, kids, and peers. Using आप with strangers is never wrong.
मेरा (meraa) = my, नाम (naam) = name, है (hai) = is. Word for word: 'my name Arjun is.'
कहाँ है with the place name gets you directions. The price question is for shopping; 'I'm fine' answers a greeting.

choices: answer about yourself — they asked 'and you?'
questions.explain: और आप? means 'and you?' — it's your turn to answer the question they just answered.

questions.q: Which sentence is a complete greeting exchange?
questions.explain: नमस्ते (hello) + आप कैसे हैं (how are you) is the classic opener. The others mash unrelated phrases together.
